headline.statement: The paper states two mutually exclusive response scales for its lead predictor -- Measures defines engaging communication on a four-point scale topping out at 4 = 'Outstanding', while Results reports its mean 'on a 1.25-5 scale' -- so the magnitude of the paper's central effect cannot be interpreted.
headline.evidence: Measures: "response options 1 = Needs a lot of work, 2 = Needs a little work, 3 = Good, 4 = Outstanding; Cronbach's alpha = 0.93". Results: "the mean level of engaging communication was 3.83 on a 1.25-5 scale, corresponding to 'good' for such facets as frequency." Table 1: "Communication (mean, SD) | 3.83 (0.42)". Under the Measures reading no coalition can exceed 4, so the proportion above 4 is necessarily 0/64; under a normal model with mean 3.83 and SD 0.42 the expected proportion above 4 is 0.3428 (binomial p = 3.03e-12). The narrative gloss compounds it: on the stated 1-4 scale, 3.83 sits nearer 'Outstanding' than 'Good'.

findings.title: Contradictory stated scale bounds for the headline predictor (engaging communication)
findings.location: Measures, 'Engaging communication' paragraph vs Results paragraph 1; Table 1 Communication row
findings.reported: Measures: four response options, 1 = 'Needs a lot of work' through 4 = 'Outstanding'. Results: "the mean level of engaging communication was 3.83 on a 1.25-5 scale, corresponding to 'good'". Table 1: 3.83 (0.42), n = 64.
findings.computed: The two statements cannot both be true. Corroboration: under a normal model with mean 3.83 / SD 0.42, the expected proportion above 4 is 0.3428, whereas the 1-4 reading forces 0/64 (binomial p = 3.03e-12, 95% CI [0, 0.056]). check_sd_range shows SD 0.42 is admissible under both readings (27.8% of the maximum possible SD of 1.512 for a 1-4 range), so dispersion cannot adjudicate which scale is correct.
findings.assumptions: The binomial corroboration assumes normality of the coalition-level aggregate; a ceiling-bounded variable would be left-skewed, which weakens that specific arithmetic (this is why I hold the finding at 'suspicious' rather than adopting the tool's own 'highly_suspicious'). The contradiction itself assumes nothing beyond the paper's own two statements. No invented range is used: both bounds are quoted from the paper.

findings.title: Table 3 baseline row: one printed estimate carries three different p-values, one of which is printed as '0'
findings.location: Table 3, 'Number of EBP at baseline' row, all three columns
findings.computed: Columns 1 and 3 print an identical coefficient and identical SE, yet report p = .01 and p < .001. Reconstructing z = B/SE = 0.01/0.002 = 5.00 and passing it to statcheck: the '<.001' cell is not flagged (computed p = 1e-06) while the '.01' cell is flagged as an error, correct_at_printed_precision = false -- identical inputs cannot legitimately give both. Column 2's p-value is printed as the literal character '0', which is not a possible p-value; this was confirmed identically in the markdown extraction and in the PDF, so it is not a transcription artefact.
findings.assumptions: Assumes the parenthesised values are standard errors and that Stata reports Wald z for poisson/nbreg (both supported: 8 of the 9 headline tests reproduce their printed p exactly under this reading). Important counterweight, and the reason this is not ranked 'impossible': the coefficient is printed to ONE significant figure, so its rounding interval against the SE interval admits z anywhere from roughly 2 to 10, and p = .01 is reachable inside that band. The underlying problem is therefore uninformative printed precision plus a formatting slip, not a demonstrated arithmetic violation.
findings.reproduction: metascience statcheck --text "Number of EBP at baseline Table 3 column 1: z = 5.00, p = .01. Number of EBP at baseline Table 3 column 3: z = 5.00, p < .001."
findings.reproduction_problem: contains placeholder '<' -- not runnable as written

findings.title: The study's randomized element is stated as a model term in every model but appears in no table and is never reported
findings.location: Methods, Covariates paragraph vs Tables 2, 3 and 4; Table 1
findings.reported: Methods: "Additionally, all models included a binary variable indicating whether the coalition was assigned to receive the full Coalition Check Up TA..." and "The final retained set of covariates, apart from Coalition Check Up treatment assignment status, were the following:". Sample: "Half of these coalitions were randomly assigned to participate in the Coalition Check-Up technical assistance (TA)."
findings.computed: No treatment-assignment row appears in Table 2, 3 or 4; the tables carry only the key predictor, Number/Quality of EBP at baseline, Communities That Care, Externally funded, Level of technical assistance, Number of members, and the Constant. Table 1 has a single 'All coalitions' column with no by-arm split and no baseline p-values, so csf_test and bayesian_table1_dispersion had nothing to consume and were correctly not run. A stated model term is therefore unverifiable, and the randomized comparison embedded in the study is invisible.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. Note the paper also says the ordinal TA-level covariate "varied between coalitions assigned to the Coalition Check-Up process and those that were not", so that covariate is partly collinear with the unreported assignment indicator -- a further reason its omission matters.

findings.title: All three results tables label regression coefficients and standard errors as 'M (SD)'
findings.reported: "| Variable | M (SD) | p | M (SD) | p | M (SD) | p |" under a spanning header reading 'Coefficient'. Results text: "Results in Tables 2-4 are shown as coefficients, and do not include effect sizes".
findings.computed: The cells are coefficients and their standard errors, not means and SDs. This is confirmed empirically rather than assumed: 8 of the 9 headline predictor tests, and 9 of 14 reconstructed tests overall, reproduce their printed p-value exactly under the B/SE reading (e.g. z = 1.81 gives p = .0703 against a printed .07; z = 0.14 gives p = .8887 against a printed .89). Verified as printed in both the markdown and the independent PDF extraction.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. A labelling error rather than a numerical one, but a reader taking the header at face value would misread every effect estimate in the paper.
findings.reproduction: metascience statcheck --text "Inclusion of community residents number of EBPs: z = 1.81, p = .07. Inclusion of community residents fidelity: z = 0.14, p = .89. Communication fidelity: z = 0.88, p = .38."

findings.title: Five of 14 reconstructed p-values disagree with their own coefficient and standard error, including one headline result
findings.location: Table 2 (Constant col 1; Level of technical assistance cols 1-2), Table 3 (Inclusive decision making col 2; Number of EBP at baseline col 1)
findings.computed: statcheck on z reconstructed as B/SE: z = 3.01 gives p = .0026 against a reported '<.001' (about 2.6x the claimed threshold, and still .0025 at the most favourable rounding z = 3.02); z = 2.83 gives p = .0047 against a reported '.01'; z = 0.06 gives p = .9522 against reported '.97' and '.98' -- two adjacent columns print an identical coefficient and SE but two different p-values. Of 14 statistics, 5 errors, 0 explained by rounding, and critically ZERO decision errors: no p-value falls on the wrong side of .05 and not one significance call flips.
findings.assumptions: Assumes parenthesised values are SEs (see rank 4) and that the tables report Wald z. The Table 3 inclusive-decision-making error runs in the CONSERVATIVE direction (true p smaller than reported), so the substantive claim is unaffected. The identical-coefficient pairs have an entirely benign explanation: unrounded values differing slightly and both rounding to two decimals. STALT was run on the two 'p<.001' claims and returned 'consistent', but that is a direction artefact -- STALT detects p-values suspiciously SMALLER than a threshold, and here the recomputed values are LARGER (orders_of_magnitude_smaller = -0.42). statcheck is the authority for these cells.
findings.reproduction: metascience statcheck --text "Constant column 1: z = 3.01, p < .001. Inclusive decision making reach: z = 2.83, p = .01. Level of technical assistance column 1: z = 0.06, p = .97. Level of technical assistance column 2: z = 0.06, p = .98."
findings.reproduction_problem: contains placeholder '<' -- not runnable as written

findings.title: The fidelity null is asserted without any interval, and the Highlights convert it into a claim that the effect exists
findings.reported: Results: "none of the inclusive leadership practices that we examined was associated with subsequent EBP fidelity (Table 4)." Table 4: Communication 0.53 (0.60) p = .38; Inclusive decision making -0.05 (0.98) p = .96; Inclusion of community residents -0.10 (0.72) p = .89; n = 101 programs in 35 coalitions. Highlights: "It is not yet clear how inclusive leadership improves evidence-based practice fidelity."
findings.computed: The three reported p-values reproduce correctly from their own coefficients and SEs (z = 0.88 -> p = .379; z = 0.05 -> p = .960; z = 0.14 -> p = .889), so the null is arithmetically sound. What could NOT be computed is the range of effects the data still permit: absence_of_evidence requires ci_low/ci_high and the paper reports no confidence interval anywhere, for any estimate. On a 1-7 fidelity outcome, standard errors of 0.60, 0.98 and 0.72 around estimates near zero are large relative to the scale, so 'no association' is an unquantified statement. No smallest effect size of interest is stated either, so equivalence could not have been claimed even if intervals were given.
findings.assumptions: Deriving a CI from B and SE would be interval arithmetic performed by hand, which is barred, so no bound is asserted here -- this finding records a reporting gap, not a computed contradiction, and is marked unverified for that reason. The Highlights wording ('how inclusive leadership improves... fidelity') presupposes an effect the paper's own data did not support; a second Highlight ('Including local residents in decision making may also improve the use of evidence-based practices') rests partly on an association the Results themselves call "only marginally significant, at p = .07".
findings.reproduction: metascience statcheck --text "Communication fidelity: z = 0.88, p = .38. Inclusive decision making fidelity: z = 0.05, p = .96. Inclusion of community residents fidelity: z = 0.14, p = .89."

findings.title: Nine primary tests with no multiplicity correction, plus a data-driven covariate screen at p < 0.10
findings.location: Analyses / Covariates sections; Tables 2-4 key predictor rows
findings.reported: Three leadership measures x three EBP outcomes = nine primary tests, reported p = .01, .03, .07, .03, .01, .03, .38, .96, .89. Covariates: "Variables were retained in the final models as covariates only if bivariate associations had p values under 0.10." No correction is stated anywhere.
findings.computed: All nine primary p-values were verified against their own coefficients and SEs via statcheck (8 of 9 correct at printed precision; the ninth errs conservatively). The five nominally significant results lie between p = .01 and p = .03. Separately, required_n indicates that detecting a moderate association (r = 0.30) at 80% power with alpha = .05 two-tailed would need 85 units against the 64 coalitions analysed.
findings.assumptions: No validated multiplicity tool exists in this toolset, so no corrected threshold is asserted as a tool output. The required_n comparison is INDICATIVE ONLY and not an exact power calculation for these models, which are Poisson/negative-binomial with six covariates rather than a simple correlation; the paper states no a-priori power analysis, so there is nothing to reproduce. Uncorrected multiplicity is entirely ordinary in this literature -- this is flagged as a design/reporting observation, not an error.

findings.title: Table 1's EBP adherence cell has no resolvable denominator, and the construct is named three different ways
findings.location: Table 1, 'EBP adherence' row; Measures 'EBP fidelity'; Table 4 'Quality of EBP at baseline'
findings.reported: "EBP adherence | 5.23 (1.13)", printed under a column headed "n = 64". Table 1 also reports "Use at least one evidence-based program (n, %) | 38 (59%)". Table 4 is titled "n = 101 programs in 35 coalitions".
findings.computed: parse_cells_typed returned kind = 'ambiguous' for this cell (candidates: mean_sd, n_percent, estimate_ci) because -- alone among Table 1's continuous rows -- the label omits the '(mean, SD)' annotation that disambiguates every other one. No forensic tool was run on it, by design. Independently, the denominator cannot be 64: adherence exists only where an EBP was delivered, and the paper reports 38 coalitions using any EBP and 35 coalitions in the fidelity model. No GRIM-family check could be given a trustworthy n.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. Running a check on a value of unknown meaning and unknown denominator is the cheapest route to a false accusation, so it is refused rather than forced. The three-way naming ('EBP adherence', 'EBP fidelity', 'Quality of EBP at baseline') is a documentary observation.
findings.reproduction_problem: contains placeholder '{' -- not runnable as written; contains placeholder '}' -- not runnable as written

not_checked.location: Table 4, all three null results (Communication B = 0.53 SE = 0.60; IDM B = -0.05 SE = 0.98; ICR B = -0.10 SE = 0.72)
not_checked.reason: The paper's headline null claim could not be evaluated with absence_of_evidence because the paper reports NO confidence intervals anywhere, and that tool requires ci_low/ci_high. Deriving a CI from B and SE would be interval arithmetic performed by hand, which is barred. No SESOI is stated either, so equivalence could not have been claimed even with intervals.

not_checked.location: Effect sizes for all nine primary tests
not_checked.reason: check_effect_plausibility could not be run: the paper explicitly declines to report standardized effect sizes ("effects are multiplicative and unit increases in key independent variables are idiosyncratic and scale-dependent"). Poisson/negative-binomial log coefficients on idiosyncratic Likert units cannot be benchmarked against the tool's empirical field distributions without a units mismatch.

not_checked.location: Baseline balance across the randomized Coalition Check-Up TA arms
not_checked.reason: csf_test and bayesian_table1_dispersion were not run because the paper reports no by-arm baseline table and no baseline p-values; Table 1 has a single 'All coalitions' column. Running either would have required inventing arm-level data. The absence is itself reported as finding rank 3.

parse_table warned of an ambiguous thousands/decimal separator and parse_cells_typed mis-typed the cell as estimate_ci. It is an unbounded continuous population count with no stated range, so GRIM, GRIMMER and SPRITE are inapplicable and check_sd_range has no defensible bound. SD exceeding the mean is unremarkable for a right-skewed population variable.
Typed as 'ambiguous' by parse_cells_typed and additionally lacking a resolvable denominator; no forensic tool was run on it. Reported in full as finding rank 8.

not_checked.location: Reliability coefficients: Cronbach's alpha 0.93 and 0.88; item correlations 0.76 and 0.80; unconditional ICC 0.10
not_checked.reason: No validated tool in this toolset verifies internal-consistency or reliability coefficients from summary statistics alone; doing so would require the item covariance matrix, which is not reported. All five values are in ordinary ranges and none is out of bounds on its face.

not_checked.location: Survey response rates: 60% (1108/1851) in Year 1 and 56% (945/1695) in Year 2
not_checked.reason: Both percentages are printed to zero decimals against denominators near 1700-1850, where GRIM has effectively no discriminating power, so grim_percentage would return a vacuous 'consistent'. Verifying the numerator-to-percentage division is plain arithmetic with no tool that performs it, so it was not asserted either way.

not_checked.location: Supporting Information S1, Tables S1 and S2 (registry hierarchy used to classify programs as EBPs)
not_checked.reason: Referenced by the paper but not supplied with the PDF or markdown body, so the EBP coding rules that determine the primary outcome could not be inspected.

not_checked.location: Sensitivity analyses omitting coalitions without EBPs
not_checked.reason: The paper states "Sensitivity analyses omitting these coalitions yielded very similar associations to those reported here" but reports no coefficients, standard errors or p-values from them, so there is nothing to check.

not_checked.location: STALT direction check on the two 'p<.001' claims (Table 2 Constant col 1; Table 3 CTC col 1)
not_checked.reason: stalt_check returned 'consistent' for both, but that verdict is a DIRECTION ARTEFACT and must not be read as endorsing the threshold claims: STALT detects p-values suspiciously SMALLER than a threshold, whereas here the recomputed p-values are LARGER (orders_of_magnitude_smaller = -0.42 and -0.11). statcheck is the authority for those cells.

SPRITE returned 'search_exhausted' over the 0-5370 integer range, not 'no_solution_proven'. Only the latter is evidence; a failed stochastic search over a range this wide tells us about the search, not the data. GRIM and GRIMMER both passed on this row.

No range-based claim is made. An initial GRIMMER/SPRITE 'impossible' on this row was an artefact of a default 1-7 scale bound that the paper never states; re-run against a defensible bound the row is GRIM- and GRIMMER-consistent. Rulebook rule 4 forbids reporting a range violation resting on an invented bound.

limitations: This agent reads text and tables only; it does not see figures. Any value appearing solely in a chart was not examined. (This paper's substantive results are all tabular, so the practical loss here is small.)

The paper reports no confidence intervals for any estimate, anywhere. This blocks the absence_of_evidence check on the fidelity null and leaves the precision of every reported association unquantified.

All NHST verification had to be routed through z-values reconstructed as B/SE from the printed coefficients and standard errors, because the narrative reports significance only as bare thresholds ('p<.05', 'p<.01') with no test statistic or df -- statcheck found zero APA-format statistics in the body text. This assumes the tables report Wald z (standard for Stata's poisson and nbreg, and for `mixed` in Table 4); if Table 4 reports t instead, its recomputed p-values would shift slightly, though none is near a decision boundary.

The continuous-to-categorical corroboration of the scale contradiction assumes normality of the coalition-level aggregate. A ceiling-bounded variable would be left-skewed, which weakens that specific arithmetic without removing the documentary contradiction it corroborates.

Several Table 3 coefficients are printed to one significant figure (0.01 with SE 0.002 or 0.001). Rows at that precision cannot be verified in principle, in either direction -- neither confirmed nor refuted.
Supporting Information S1 (Tables S1 and S2, the registry hierarchy defining the primary outcome) was not supplied and could not be inspected.

No raw data were available. The data availability statement offers the datasets "from Drs. Brown and Chilenski upon reasonable request" rather than through deposit, so none of the findings above can be settled by re-analysis.

tables_checked: Table 1 (coalition EBPs, inclusive leadership and other attributes, n=64)
Table 2 (inclusive leadership -> number of EBPs, Poisson, n=64)
Table 3 (inclusive leadership -> EBP reach, negative binomial, n=64)
Table 4 (inclusive leadership -> EBP fidelity, mixed model, 101 programs in 35 coalitions)

report_markdown:
## What the paper claims

Wells and colleagues follow 64 youth substance-misuse prevention coalitions in Pennsylvania and Missouri across two annual waves, nested inside a NIDA-funded randomized technical-assistance trial. They ask whether three facets of inclusive coalition leadership at Wave 1 -- engaging communication, inclusive decision making, and inclusion of community residents -- predict use of evidence-based practices a year later. Poisson models are fitted for the number of EBPs, negative binomial models for EBP reach, and a two-level model for implementation fidelity, each adjusted for the baseline outcome and five covariates. The reported pattern is tidy: communication and inclusive decision making predict more EBPs; all three predict greater reach; none predicts fidelity.

## What held up

The arithmetic that can be checked largely checks out, and this matters for how the rest of the review should be read. Table 1's seven two-decimal percentages jointly admit only n = 64, 128 or 192 as denominators, and each recovers exactly the count printed beside it at n = 64 (55/64, 9/64, 26/64, 41/64, 23/64, 21/64, 20/64). GRIM, GRIMMER and SPRITE all pass on the EBP count row against the paper's own stated 0-9 range. Every dispersion value sits comfortably inside its instrument bound. A cross-table duplication scan over all 63 coefficient cells found zero identical (mean, SD) pairs across 1160 comparisons; the six near-matches are digit transpositions between trivially small round values and were discounted. Sample sizes show natural non-round variation (68 coalitions dropping to 64, 101 programs, 1108/1851 and 945/1695 survey responses). And across 14 regression results reconstructed from their own coefficients and standard errors, statcheck found **zero decision errors** -- not one significance call flips. Nothing in this paper points at fabricated data.

Two sweep flags I discarded on inspection. A GRIMMER/SPRITE "impossible" on the coalition-size row (35.78, SD 33.74) was an artefact of a default 1-7 scale that the paper never states; re-run against a defensible bound the row passes, and rulebook rule 4 forbids any range claim there. A SPRITE failure on EBP reach returned `search_exhausted`, not `no_solution_proven` -- a failed stochastic search over a 0-5370 integer range tells us about the search. I also declined two statcheck flags (Table 3 Communities That Care, Table 4 baseline quality) that are fully explained by the precision at which their inputs were printed.

## Why the paper is nonetheless hard to trust as printed

The problems here are of a different kind from data-integrity anomalies. This paper is difficult to verify not because its numbers conflict with each other but because too many of them are printed too coarsely, labelled wrongly, or not printed at all.

Consider what a reader needs to size the headline effect. The paper explicitly declines to report standardized effect sizes -- "effects are multiplicative and unit increases in key independent variables are idiosyncratic and scale-dependent" -- which is a defensible choice. But it makes the raw coefficient the only available yardstick, and a raw coefficient is meaningless without a known predictor scale. That is precisely what the Measures/Results contradiction removes. Compounding it, the observed SDs of the three predictors are small (0.42, 0.29, 0.32), so no coalition in this sample moves anywhere near a full scale point: a coefficient of 1.34 log-EBPs per unit of inclusive decision making describes a contrast that does not occur in the data. With no confidence intervals anywhere in the paper, neither the positive findings nor the fidelity null carries a stated range of compatible effects.

The fidelity null deserves particular care, because the paper's own Highlights quietly convert it into a promissory note: "It is not yet clear *how* inclusive leadership improves evidence-based practice fidelity" presupposes that it does. What the data show is three coefficients near zero with standard errors of 0.60, 0.98 and 0.72 on a seven-point outcome, from 101 programs in 35 coalitions. That is a small, imprecise study reporting an unquantified absence of evidence. A second Highlight -- "Including local residents in decision making may also improve the use of evidence-based practices" -- rests in part on an association the Results themselves describe as "only marginally significant, at p = .07".

The randomized element is the strangest omission. Half of the original 68 coalitions were randomly assigned to the Coalition Check-Up TA; the Methods state the assignment indicator was in every model; it appears in no table. Because Table 1 carries a single "All coalitions" column with no arm-level split and no baseline p-values, the baseline-similarity tests (Carlisle-Stouffer-Fisher, Table-1 dispersion) had nothing to consume and were not run. That is a gap in coverage, not a clean bill of health, and I have recorded it as such rather than reporting reassurance the data cannot support.

Finally, the analysis has more forking paths than are acknowledged: nine primary tests across three exposures and three outcomes with no multiplicity adjustment, and covariates chosen by a bivariate screen at p < 0.10. The five nominally significant primary results sit between p = .01 and p = .03. No a-priori power analysis is reported. The data are offered "from Drs. Brown and Chilenski upon reasonable request" rather than deposited -- ordinary for this journal, but it does mean none of the above can be settled by re-analysis.

## Verdict

I see no sign of fabricated or manipulated data, and the substantive conclusions may well be sound. But as printed, the results tables are mislabelled, internally inconsistent in places, and in several rows too coarse to check at all, and the paper's most-quoted predictor sits on a scale the paper contradicts itself about. I would want the communication scale clarified, the treatment-assignment coefficient reported, and every estimate re-printed at full precision with confidence intervals before relying on these numbers.
